title: How The Eye of a Tornado Works
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant discuss tornadoes, starting with Josh's experience growing up in Toledo, Ohio near tornado alley and tornadoes in Atlanta. They explain how a tornado forms (a horizontal spinning tube of wind tilted upright by rising air), debunk myths (tornadoes are not visible wind but debris and dust; opening windows does not protect a house; low pressure does not make houses explode, flying debris is the danger), and recommend NOAA advice to keep windows closed and go to the basement. They then recount the two known cases of people who were in the eye of a tornado: a Kansas farmer named Keller in 1943 who stayed to watch the storm and was enveloped, and a Texas farmer named Roy Hall who went into his house as the tornado tore off its roof and found himself in the eye. Both describe calm, smooth walls, constant lightning, and small twisters hissing along the walls. The Texas storm reportedly killed a hundred people in the town. The episode is a promo-bracketed short piece, with a pointer to a How Stuff Works article on the eye of a tornado.

segments.title: Opening banter and tornado experiences
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the show. Josh talks about growing up in Toledo, Ohio, seeing tornadoes, and recent tornadoes that hit downtown Atlanta. They say few people have been in a tornado's eye.

segments.title: How tornadoes form
segments.summary: Josh explains that a thunderstorm's rising air tilts a horizontal spinning wind tube upright, creating the vertical tornado, which can reach very high wind speeds.

segments.title: Tornado myths and safety
segments.summary: The hosts say tornadoes are visible only through the debris and dust they pick up, not the wind itself. They debunk the myths that opening windows helps and that low pressure makes houses explode; flying debris is the real danger. NOAA advises keeping windows closed and going to the basement.

segments.title: Farmer Keller's 1943 encounter
segments.summary: A Kansas farmer named Keller saw a tornado approaching, got his family into the storm cellar, but stayed to watch and was lifted into the tornado's calm, lightning-lit interior, where small twisters hissed along the walls.

segments.title: Roy Hall's Texas tornado and sign-off
segments.summary: A Texas farmer, Roy Hall, went into his house as a tornado tore off the roof and found himself in the eye with similar calm, smooth walls and lightning. The Texas storm reportedly killed a hundred people in the town. The hosts point listeners to a How Stuff Works article and sign off.
